title: StarClear
question: How does a star shine?
hook: Every second the Sun turns about 4 million tonnes of itself into light. Open a star, watch hydrogen fuse into helium, follow light on its thousands-of-years walk out, and see how a star's mass decides its colour, its life and its death.

explainer.title: A ball of gas in balance
explainer.text: A star is a huge ball of hot gas. Gravity pulls it inward; the pressure of hot, squeezed gas pushes out. Where the two match, the star holds steady for billions of years.

explainer.title: Fusion in the core
explainer.text: At about 15 million K, hydrogen nuclei fuse. Step by step, four of them become one helium nucleus that weighs about 0.7% less. The missing mass becomes energy, E = mc².

explainer.title: A wall and a tunnel
explainer.text: Protons repel each other, and few have the energy to get close. Quantum tunnelling lets a small fraction slip through the barrier anyway. Heavier stars mostly use the CNO cycle instead.

explainer.title: The long walk out
explainer.text: Light from the core is absorbed and re-emitted countless times. Estimates for how long energy takes to leave the radiative zone range from about 10,000 to 170,000 years. Convection then carries it up, and from the surface it reaches Earth in about 8 minutes 20 seconds.

explainer.title: Mass sets colour and brightness
explainer.text: Heavier stars have hotter cores, burn far faster and look bluer. Red stars are about 3,000 K, blue ones above 20,000 K. On the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram most stars sit on the main sequence.

explainer.title: How stars end
explainer.text: The Sun is about 4.6 billion years into a roughly 10-billion-year life. It will become a red giant and then a white dwarf. Stars above about 8 Suns explode as supernovas, leaving neutron stars or black holes, and scatter the elements we are made of.
